item.title: Stop Telling Caregivers to Take Care of Themselves
item.description:
Caregiving

Stop Telling Caregivers to Take Care of Themselves

Personal Perspective: Ask caregivers what they need.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • People have complex, multidimensional needs.
  • Difficulty identifying emotions can lead to unidentified and unmet needs.
  • Asking others what they need is much more compassionate than telling them to take care of themselves.

"What do you need?"

I asked this question about a million times as a support group co-facilitator, usually while gesturing toward the poster outlining the predictable "emotional stages of reactions." Each phase detailed a level of challenge that individuals and families affected by mental illness face, along with accompanying needs, as we walked through the varying storms that brought us to group. Narrowing down what might help proved difficult and vital.

It's been years since I co-facilitated these groups. Yet, I find myself asking the same question.

"What do you need?"

I have charts in my office detailing common emotions and corresponding needs. Sometimes I will hand a client a stack of feeling cards and go from there.

When caught in a whirlwind, a seemingly simple question like this can become quite complex.

As my father has been facing advanced-stage cancer, I have been asking myself this same question. The same things that made the question so valuable then make the question valuable now, both for him and me.

More Than An Illness—More Than a Caregiver

I have mixed feelings about the term "caregiver," as it implies just one role a person is playing in their life, and just one role the person they are caring for is playing as well.

When someone cares for someone, that person they are looking out for may have a kaleidoscope of other roles. My dad was once a kid who snuck a rabbit into the house and a technician who became friends with every local bar owner because his job was fixing jukeboxes. He’s still that same person—not just a person with cancer. He's my dad.

Why "Take Care of Yourself" Isn't Always Helpful

“Take care of yourself” is often a song sung to people going through a hard time. For caregivers, sometimes it turns into, “You need to take care of yourself.”

Though perhaps well-meaning, those words are not helpful.

Telling someone “You need to take care of yourself” deeply oversimplifies complicated emotions and realities. It also puts the onus of responsibility back on a person whose responsibility has been deeply extended.

It does little for someone in a caregiver’s role; rather, it literally tells them to take care of it themselves. They are overwhelmed. They're pressed for time. They are usually caring for everyone as best as they can, including themselves.

What Do You Need?

Here’s what you can do instead: Ask, "What do you need?"

article continues after advertisement

Then listen.

Needs are complex. The great psychologist Abraham Maslow offered us a hierarchy of needs, which included physiological needs, safety needs, belonging needs, need for achievement (which others have reconceptualized as meaning), and self-actualization. Still, when it comes to major health issues, the question becomes even more complex.

For example, a person may be living with schizophrenia, but their needs reach far beyond any diagnosis; perhaps, like too many, they are struggling with housing. The initial need is quite tangible: a place to live. Yet, like an accordion, it expands. They may need a place to live and the sense of security that comes from having a home base. They may also crave the comfort of home and the feeling of belonging that comes with it.

Someone who loves them and is in a role of providing support will have complex, winding needs as well. Indeed, they are not the person who is living with schizophrenia or experiencing homelessness, yet they need to know that this person they love and value has their needs met. Our needs are not always just our own.

You don't have to grant every need, and they don't have to have an answer for you. Still, it does a whole lot more than telling someone to take care of themselves. The question is powerful in itself.

item.title: The Final Two Steps to Alleviating Abusive Behavior
item.description:
Emotional Abuse

The Final Two Steps to Alleviating Abusive Behavior

How to give a meaningful apology and complete your unfinished business.

Posted July 28, 2026

Key points
  • A meaningful apology consists of what I refer to as the 3 Rs: regret, responsibility, and remedy.
  • In order to truly feel regret we must be able to have empathy for those we have harmed.
  • The final step—processing the traumas that created your abusiveness—will be ongoing.

These are the final steps in my seven-step process for healing abusive behavior.

Step 6: Learn how to give a meaningful apology and experience empathy

In the previous step (#5), you were asked to acknowledge to your partner (or older child) that your behavior has sometimes been abusive. The next step is for you to apologize for that behavior. Apologizing to your partner (or older child) for your abusive behavior or attitude will not only be healing for them, but for you as well. We are not talking about just any apology; we are talking about what I call a meaningful apology. A meaningful apology consists of what I call the three Rs of apology—regret, responsibility, and remedy. Unless all three of these elements are present, your partner will sense that something is missing in your apology and they will feel short-changed. Let’s take a look at each element in detail:

  • Regret—a statement of regret for having caused hurt and damage to the other person. This includes an expression of empathy toward the other person, including an acknowledgement of the hurt and damage you caused this person.
  • Responsibility—an acceptance of responsibility for your actions. This means not blaming anyone else for what you did and not making excuses for your actions, but instead accepting full responsibility for what you did and for the consequences of your actions.
  • Remedy—a statement of your willingness to take action to remedy the situation. This takes place either by promising not to repeat the action, promising to work toward not making the same mistake again, stating how you are going to remedy the situation (e.g., go to therapy), or making restitution for the damages you caused (e.g., paying for your partner’s therapy).

Practicing Empathy

Before you can give a meaningful apology—an apology that will be truly healing to both of you—you must first develop empathy for your partner. This can be difficult for some of you. The following exercise will help:

  1. Start by imagining how your partner must have felt when you treated them the way you did. Do you think they felt hurt? Angry? Afraid? Ashamed? Disappointed?
  2. Now think about the effects your abusive behavior had on your partner’s self-esteem. Can you understand how your words or actions damaged their self-image?
  3. If you denied responsibility for your abusive actions or tried to make your partner doubt their perceptions, can you imagine how this would have affected them?
  4. How do you imagine it must have felt to live with you? Can you imagine how hopeless your partner must have felt at times? Can you imagine how much they must have hated you and hated themselves for not being able to leave you?
article continues after advertisement

If you have difficulty putting yourself in your partner’s place, don’t get discouraged. Keep trying. It will certainly help if you are willing to listen to your partner tell you how much you hurt or damaged them. The more you are open to truly taking in what those you harmed have to say, the more empathy you will develop. One very effective tool is to write about your relationship from your partner’s point of view (“I’m __’s partner and this is how it has felt to be involved with him”). Think of empathy as a skill or a muscle. The more you practice it, the stronger it will become.

Step 7: Continue to work on your unfinished business from the past

This includes continuing to release your feelings of anger and pain toward those who harmed you and confronting abusers, either directly or indirectly.

You may find that you continue to resist the idea that it was the neglect or abuse by one of your parents (or other significant caregivers) that set you up to become abusive. Ironically, those who become abusive often have a more difficult time admitting this than other people. While it is natural to want to protect your parents, do not do so at the expense of your own healing. Working on your unfinished business includes:

  • Acknowledging the anger, sadness, fear, and shame you feel as a result of the neglect or abuse you experienced as a child. For example, while you may have no difficulty getting angry at your partner, your anger toward an abuser may be buried deep inside of you. Fortunately, you can use your current anger to help you access your repressed or suppressed anger from the past. Every time you get angry at your partner, ask yourself if one of your parents displayed the same behavior that is upsetting you concerning your partner. For example, if your partner is too busy with kids to stop and listen to you, ask yourself if this reminds you of how your mother ignored your needs.
  • Find safe and constructive ways to release your anger and pain concerning your childhood abuse (e.g., kneel down beside your bed and hit your mattress with your fists, put your head in a pillow and scream).
  • Confront your abuser or abusers (not necessarily in person). For example, write them a letter (that you do not send) telling them how they harmed you and how you feel about what they did. When you are alone in the house, tell your abusive parent off, saying everything you wish you could have said at the time.
article continues after advertisement

I hope these seven steps have helped you in your desire to discontinue your abusive behavior. These steps may seem simple, but the work you put into practicing them will be difficult at times. You’ll want to talk yourself out of facing painful memories and emotions, but this is the key to healing. Your pride may tell you that it wasn’t your fault that you became abusive, that your partner played a role as well. But in this case, your pride is just a way of covering up your shame—shame that can be healed by doing the work. I wish you all the best for your healing journey.
